newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Afghan women refugees wary of returning home.
newsitem.headline: Afghan women refugees wary of returning home.

text.p: Relief workers are trying to persuade Afghan refugees to return home after the Islamic Taleban militia took Kabul last week, but many women refugees said on Tuesday they were afraid of the new rulers.
In this sprawling makeshift refugee township inside Pakistan, women who fled the horrors of 17 years of war said the Taleban's strict fundamentalist limits on women would make life impossible.

"Nowhere in the world is there a government which stops women from working and makes them stay home. We want to work. This government should give us rights," Razia Barakzai, a teacher from Kabul who fled to the border in 1994, told Reuters.
Busloads of refugees began returning on Monday after tensions along the border eased in the wake of last week's Taleban takeover of Kabul, officials based in Pakistan said.

But officials of the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees said they were part of a recent influx and not among the hundreds of thousands of long-term refugees who have fled fighting and hardship in the conflict.
For them this camp of mud huts has been home, and for some a birthplace, and women such as Barakzai have built schools to educate its teeming youth.

The Taleban promise to govern Afghanistan, three quarters of which they now control, according to Islamic Sharia law, including punishments such as death for murder, stoning for adultery and amputation for theft.
A six-man interim ruling shura (council) has ordered men to report for work, but has yet to announce if and when women will be allowed to resume their jobs.

Wearing a traditional Islamic shawl, Toorpakay Waismahmoodi echoed the thoughts of women inside and outside the country when she said it would be impossible for them to survive at home, given the toll inflicted on families by the war.
"We are educated. I worked in Kabul as well. My father is dead...and I have a brother and three sisters. If I don't work who is going to look after us?" she said in an interview.

Overhead, Pakistani jet fighters undertook manoeuvres along the still tense border with Afghanistan near the Khyber Pass and the city of Jalalabad, the scene of recent bombing by forces loyal to ousted president Burhanuddin Rabbani.
In the camp, throngs of children excited by the presence of a foreign film crew laughed and joked as young men queued at one of the camp's few water pumps to collect supplies.
The officer overseeing this and other camps in Peshawar, Younas Khan, told Reuters most of some 10,000 new arrivals were expected to return soon to Afghanistan.

"We are not expecting any further arrivals, in fact we are expecting these refugees to go back home, since there are no threats of any bombardment and the Taleban have already declared peace in Afghanistan, especially in Jalalabad," he said.
But the future of long-stayers, particularly the women, was not so clear.
"We can never go back if there are no jobs for us... They should let us go back when there is peace and whichever group is in place in Kabul, they should let us work," said Barakzai.
